Case Information: A 76-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-year history of a recurrent itchy rash on the hips, thighs, and under the breasts, accompanied by intermittent lesions resembling vesicles and bullae. Previous treatments with topical and intralesional corticosteroids provided minimal relief. The patient also experienced swelling in the lower extremities. She had a history of long-standing severe lichen sclerosis et atrophicus. Several months before the onset of the rash, she underwent radical vulvectomy and bilateral inguino-femoral lymph node dissection for stage 2/grade 2 invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva. Physical examination revealed multiple erosions with hemorrhagic crusts and multiple clustered translucent papules on the inframammary breasts, abdomen, hips, and proximal thighs. Both legs exhibited 4+ pitting and nonpitting edema along with scattered small vesicular lesions.
Diagnostic Tests: Biopsies from representative lesions showed superficial dermal thin-walled dilated vascular channels surrounded by hyalinized collagen and scant perivascular lymphohistiocytic inflammation. The ectatic vessels showed endothelial cell staining with D2-40. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin was negative.

Case Information: An eight-month-old female infant, born at term to non-consanguineous parents, presented with multiple hypopigmented skin lesions on the trunk and extremities since birth. Initially, these appeared as linear erosions that healed within a few days, leaving behind hypopigmentation with hyperpigmented borders. The perinatal period was uneventful. Limb and nail abnormalities were noted from birth, and developmental milestones were delayed. The patient had a history of exomphalos minor, which was surgically corrected, and an atrial septal defect that closed spontaneously by three months of age. No similar symptoms were reported in siblings or other family members. General examination showed microcephaly, hypertelorism, megalopinna, low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge, and a pointed chin. Skin examination revealed multiple hypopigmented atrophic linear streaks and macules of varying sizes on the forehead, neck, trunk, thighs, gluteal region, genitalia, and upper and lower limbs, following the lines of Blaschko. There was syndactyly of the left foot and ectrodactyly (lobster claw deformity) of the right foot. The patient had supernumerary nipples and a few skin-colored growths over the proximal nail fold of the right middle finger and right foot. Nails were dystrophic, while hair and oral mucosa were normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count and serum chemistry profile were within normal limits.
Diagnostic Tests: Skin biopsy on the trunk showed focal spongiosis, occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary edema, and focal papillary dermal fibrosis with superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.

Case Information: A 23-year-old male presented with breathing difficulties and weight loss persisting for 8 months. Dermatology consultation was requested for skin lesions. Physical examination revealed pallor and enlarged submandibular and occipital lymph nodes. Skin examination identified multiple erythematous papules and nodules on the trunk, face, and scalp, with ulceration and scarring in both axillae. Some lesions had central umbilication and others were covered with adherent scales. Bronchial breath sounds were noted over the lower chest bilaterally with occasional crepitations. Peripheral blood smear showed normocytic normochromic red blood cells, neutrophilic leucocytosis, and relative lymphopenia, with no atypical cells or blasts. Hemoglobin was 8.5 gm/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 37 mm/hour, C-reactive protein was 10.2 mg/L, and total serum protein was 4.8 gms/dL. High-resolution computed tomography of the thorax revealed multiple bullae with panlobular emphysematous right residual lung and left-sided mild pleural effusion. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed multiple complex cystic and solid lesions in the liver, mildly coarsened hepatic echotexture, and minimal ascites. Non-contrast computed tomography of the brain and skull showed an intact bony calvarium with no other abnormalities. Fine needle aspiration cytology from the lymph node revealed reactive lymphoid cells.
Diagnostic Tests: Biopsies from the trunk papules as well as from the right axillary ulcerative lesion revealed intermediate-sized cells arranged in nodules in the dermis and in perivascular locations. These cells had bland chromatin with nuclear indentation and grooves with abundant cytoplasm. Epidermotropism was present with occasional mitosis. No eosinophils were seen. On immunohistochemistry (IHC), the atypical cells were strongly positive for CD1a. S100 and CD4 were strongly positive in a few of these cells and, CD68 was positive in few superficial cells only. Langerin and myeloperoxidase (MPO) were negative in these cells.

Case Information: A 69-year-old Caucasian woman reported new visual disturbances in her left eye, which began approximately ten weeks prior to her visit to the uveitis clinic in March 2023. She experienced new floaters and central flashing initially, followed by the development of an enlarging scotoma and progressive vision loss about four weeks later. Four weeks before the onset of these ocular symptoms, she tested positive for COVID-19 antibodies and experienced fever, congestion, and cough. She had received the COVID-19 vaccination several months before contracting the infection. Her medical history includes asthma, hypothyroidism, and headaches. There is no notable family history or prior autoimmune disease.
Diagnostic Tests: FAF showed peripapillary and macular hyper-autofluorescent spots in the posterior pole. These spots co-localized to punctate hyperfluorescent areas on FA, arranged in a wreath-like pattern with nearly well-defined borders. OCT examination featured disruption of the ellipsoid zone (EZ) and hyper-reflective subretinal deposits in the affected left eye.

Case Information: A seven-month-old male child presented with asymmetry in the size of the eyes, with the left eye being smaller than the right. He was born at full term to parents who are first cousins, following an uneventful pregnancy and normal vaginal delivery. Ocular examination revealed a smaller left eyelid, and upon retracting the eyelids, the socket was found to be empty. The right eye appeared normal. Systemic examination identified multiple congenital anomalies, including a head circumference of 34 cm (below the third percentile for his age), abnormalities in the external ear and fingers, hydrocele, and hypospadias. The left ear was malformed with hypoplasia of the antihelices, fusion of the helix with the tragus, and an obscured external auditory canal opening. The left hand had four normal digits and a pre-axial duplication of the thumb, while the right hand was normal. The child was unable to sit with support, potentially due to kyphosis of the thoracic vertebral column. Dental abnormalities and cognitive impairment could not be excluded.
Diagnostic Tests: Computed tomography scan of the orbit and brain showed absence of left eye in the bony socket with rudimentary optic nerve seen in the orbit and extending for a short distance into the cranium. There was hypoplasia of optic chiasma and aplasia of the entire visual pathway on the left side. The right side of the optic nerve was normal.

Case Information: An 18-year-old male presented with multiple painless skin swellings located on the right cheek, chin, eyelid, and suprapubic region. The swelling on the right cheek had been recurring for 4 years. The patient had a history of recurrent cardiac swellings in the left atrium and right ventricle, for which he had undergone surgery twice. He also experienced a cerebrovascular accident. There was no notable family history. On physical examination, the swelling on the right cheek measured 15 x 8 x 6 cm, was firm, non-tender, mobile, and not attached to underlying structures. The overlying skin was nodular and had areas of ulceration. The swellings on the right eyelid, chin, and suprapubic region measured 0.5 cm, 2.0 cm, and 3.5 cm, respectively. Additionally, there was a small pigmented lesion on the inner canthus of the right eye, multiple pigmented macules on the left shin, and several nevi on the legs and back. The patient also had vitiligo on the prepuce. Endocrine evaluation showed elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels at 48.5 pg/mL.
Diagnostic Tests: The aspirate was thick, viscous, stringy, and gelatinous. The smears were paucicellular and revealed abundant myxoid material in the background which stained magenta with Giemsa and pale blue green with Papanicolaou stain. It was admixed with hypocellular fragments of spindle and stellate cells with oval to spindle nuclei having evenly dispersed, fine chromatin, thin nuclear membrane, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Focal mild nuclear pleomorphism was noted. Mitosis and necrosis were absent. Few fragments showed thin delicate vascular cores. Epithelial structures were not seen. There were no cytologic features of malignancy. On gross examination, the cheek mass measured 15 cm × 13 cm × 6 cm. Overlying skin was focally ulcerated. On cut-surface, it was well-circumscribed, nodular, solid, gelatinous with few cystic and hemorrhagic areas. Microscopic examination revealed a tumor in the dermis and subcutaneous plane which was composed of multiple hypocellular nodules with abundant myxoid stroma and spindle to stellate cells within it. Focally, increased cellularity was seen. The cells had bland nuclear morphology and lacked cytological atypia. Mitosis and necrosis were absent. Focal areas of capillary proliferation, epithelial proliferation, and cystic changes were also seen. The eyelid lesion also showed similar morphology.

Case Information: A 36-year-old male with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss was referred to the Department of Radiology. He is the first of two brothers born to healthy parents of Turkish descent, who are first cousins. The younger brother is healthy. There is no other family history of deafness in the extended family. At the age of 9 months, the hearing impairment was noticed. An audiologic assessment confirmed severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and the loss was corrected with a hearing aid. Hearing loss has remained stable. He had no school problems and graduated from high school. On physical examination, he has no dysmorphic features. He has neither an obvious neurological difficulty nor a cognitive impairment.
Diagnostic Tests: Sagittal FLAIR images demonstrated corpus callosum hypogenesis. The rostrum, genu, and splenic portions of the corpus callosum were absent, and the body part was seen as a short thin line. Lateral ventricles were noted to be slightly small in caliper and slit like in coronal T2-weighted images. There were bilateral frontal parasagittal polymicrogyria. Nodular gray matter heterotopia was present in periventricular regions. In the inferior aspects of both cerebellar hemispheres, there were abnormal foliation and fissuration with loss of the normal architecture, consistent with cerebellar dysplasia.

Case Information: A 4-day-old full-term male infant, born to a 19-year-old mother, was admitted to the neonatal ICU due to bilious vomiting and delayed passage of meconium. Physical examination revealed discoloration of the forehead hair, eyes, and right forearm. An erect abdominal X-ray showed an air-fluid level indicative of intestinal obstruction. Blood tests indicated elevated coagulation parameters, urea, and creatinine levels. Initial management included nasogastric (NG) tube decompression and nil per os (NPO) status. Following correction of laboratory abnormalities, surgical intervention was performed. A right supra-umbilical transverse incision was made, and the entire intestine was examined. No atresia was found; however, a normal caliber intestine was observed up to the terminal ileum, where a reduction in caliber was noted. The lumen was confirmed to be patent. The large bowel appeared normal, and the abdomen was closed. Over the next 8 days, spontaneous stool passage did not occur, and bilious drainage continued via the NG tube.
Diagnostic Tests: Contrast clongraphy revealed a narrowed colon to the terminal ileum.

Case Information: A 24-year-old male reported experiencing an itchy, softened plaque primarily located in the left perineal area, which has been present since he was 5 years old and has shown periods of worsening and improvement. The affected area extends from the perineal region to the scrotum and the inner part of the left thigh. A comprehensive examination did not reveal any other abnormalities in the body. There was no notable family history.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathology revealed hyperkeratosis with a characteristic alternating orthokeratosis, hypergranulosis with parakeratosis and agranulosis along with upperdermal lymphocytic infiltrate.

Case Information: A 37-year-old woman reported experiencing pain in her right leg for six months and in her left leg for four weeks. The pain in the left leg was mild, whereas the pain in the right leg had progressively worsened. She had previously been treated with antibiotics for low-grade osteomyelitis based on radiographic features, but her symptoms did not improve, leading to her referral to our institution. There was no family history of similar conditions. General examination showed no abnormalities. Local examination revealed mild tenderness without significant findings. Routine blood tests were normal. A frontal radiograph of both legs showed sclerosis and cortical thickening in the diaphyses of both tibias, more pronounced on the right side. A CT scan indicated circumferential cortical thickening with nearly complete replacement of the medullary cavity. MRI findings were consistent, showing bone marrow edema and minimal adjacent soft tissue inflammation. A whole-body Tc-99 m methylene diphosphonate (MDP) bone scan revealed focal areas of increased tracer uptake in both tibial diaphyses, more prominent on the right side, with no other areas of increased uptake in the skeleton.
Diagnostic Tests: Biopsy from the right tibial diaphysis showed cortical thickening with packed trabeculae.

Case Information: A 57-year-old Hispanic male presented for retinal evaluation due to a progressive decline in central vision in both eyes over 7 months, more pronounced in the right eye. He reported difficulty reading, watching TV, and experiencing bilateral light sensitivity. He denied any new visual distortions, floaters, flashing lights, head or eye trauma, prior eye surgeries, or a history of strabismus or amblyopia. His ophthalmic history was notable only for poor night vision since childhood. Family history was negative for retinal diseases, and his children and grandchildren reported no night vision issues. His general medical history included well-controlled hypertension managed with lisinopril. On examination, visual acuity was counting fingers at 4 feet in the right eye and 3 feet in the left eye. Anterior segment examination, pupillary reflexes, and extraocular movements were normal. Dilated fundus examination and ultra-wide-field confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy revealed significant macular atrophy in both eyes with 3+ diffuse, fine, yellow flecks. Green wavelength fundus autofluorescence showed bull's eye maculopathy and hyperautofluorescent perifoveal rings bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography indicated foveal atrophy of the outer retina extending from the ellipsoid layer to the outer plexiform layer, with scattered hyper-reflective lesions in the peripheral macula corresponding to the flecks observed on fundoscopy. Visual field testing was unreliable due to high fixation losses bilaterally. Full-field ERG and multifocal ERG showed severely diminished responses in both eyes to scotopic flash, photopic flash, and 30 Hz flicker stimulation conditions, indicating severe electroretinal dysfunction of both rod and cone systems, with greater impairment of rod function. Multifocal ERG results indicated severe electroretinal dysfunction of the cone system within the central 30 degrees surrounding the fovea.
Diagnostic Tests: Our patient was heterozygous for two variants in the RDH5 gene: a known pathogenic variant, c.160C > T (p.Arg54), and a novel variant of presumed pathogenicity, c.814_815del (p.Leu272Aspfs63).

Case Information: A 48-year-old woman reported experiencing floaters, flashes of light, blurred vision, and eye pain in both eyes for several days before her visit. She had a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus and was on glibenclamide and metformin. Examination showed visual acuity of 20/160 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye, with no significant refractive error. Both pupils reacted normally, and there was no afferent pupillary defect. Slit lamp examination revealed 1+ cell presence in the anterior chamber, pigmentation on the anterior lens capsule, 2+ nuclear sclerosis, and 1+ to 2+ vitreous cells in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was measured at 16 mmHg in both eyes. Fundus examination identified multiple well-defined creamy-yellow subretinal lesions primarily located in the equatorial and peripapillary regions, along with dot and blot retinal hemorrhages, macular edema, and extensive neovascularization of the optic discs.
Diagnostic Tests: Fluorescein angiography (FA) demonstrated early hypo- and late hyperfluorescence of the lesions. Apart from diffuse optic disc leakage, macular leakage was also notable. On indocyanine green (ICG) angiography, the lesions remained hypofluorescent through all phases of the angiogram.

Case Information: A 30-year-old obese Caucasian female presented to the emergency department with fatigue persisting for three months. She reported recent episodes of dizziness, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath during physical activity. Additionally, she experienced diffuse, relapsing-remitting lower abdominal pain over the same period. The patient had initially consulted her obstetrician-gynecologist, who referred her to the emergency department for further evaluation of anemia based on lab results. She denied nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, melena, dysphagia, or recent weight loss. However, she admitted to occasionally seeing blood in her stools, which she noted as typical for her. She was admitted for further evaluation and red blood cell transfusion. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness upon palpation of the abdomen, with no abdominal guarding, rebound tenderness, or palpable masses. Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation was observed on her upper and lower lips, with no other significant skin lesions or physical findings. The patient had a history of hospitalization at five years old due to uncontrollable vomiting, during which she was evaluated for her condition. There was no family history of similar conditions, cancers, or gastrointestinal issues. Genetic screening at 24 years old during her first pregnancy confirmed a mutation, although her son's genetic test was negative for the same mutation. Upon presentation, the patient was afebrile with a blood pressure of 147/86 mmHg and a pulse of 109 bpm. Laboratory results showed low levels of red blood cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and mean corpuscular volume, with high total iron-binding capacity and low iron saturation percentage. Fecal occult blood testing was positive. Hemoglobin and hematocrit levels were monitored every 12 hours. The patient received two units of packed red blood cells and an iron infusion. Gastroenterology was consulted.
Diagnostic Tests: An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed hundreds of polyps in the proximal body of the stomach, with the largest measuring 3 mm. Antral inflammation was also noted. The duodenal bulb and second portion of the duodenum revealed no abnormalities. Antral and gastric biopsies were negative for Helicobacter pylori.

Case Information: A 64-year-old Caucasian woman presented with ulcers on both sides of her lower legs, which had been present for approximately 1 year and developed without any external trauma. Doppler sonography showed pronounced superficial varicosis. The patient also had pre-existing type 2 diabetes and arterial hypertension, which were considered as factors affecting wound healing. Physical examination revealed two ulcers, each about 4 cm in diameter, on the right lower leg and one ulcer, 6 cm in diameter, on the left lower leg. Signs of chronic venous insufficiency, such as corona phlebectatica and symmetrical oedema after standing, were observed. The ulcers were located proximally, and there was significant itching. The skin around the wounds showed follicular-bound, pinehead-sized, erythematous maculae and papules. Similar skin changes were noted on the thighs and upper back.
Diagnostic Tests: Histological analyses of a representative follicle revealed a pronounced infiltration of predominantly CD3+CD4+ T helper cells gathering around the adnexal structures. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells or CD20+ B cells were detected only to a small extent. The T-cell γ receptor rearrangement revealed a biclonal peak at 198 and 227 base pairs. Similar findings were observed in specimens of the ulcers.

Case Information: A 16-year-old female patient exhibited a 10.5 × 8.0 cm grayish-depressed plaque with hypochromic areas on the lower half of her left thigh lateral. Telangiectatic vessels were observed around the periphery of the lesion, with visible veins nearby. The plaque has been present since birth, initially appearing violet and gradually becoming whitened and depressed over time. There is no difference in the length of the lower limbs.
Diagnostic Tests: Angioresonance showed a vascular malformation on the skin and subcutaneous tissue supplied by non-dilated intermuscular branches tributary from the popliteal artery. Precocious venous filling was found both in the region and malformation, suggesting precocious venous shunt. Dilated drainage veins have not been documented, except for a superficial drainage vein that courses along the subcutaneous cellular tissue of the anterior thigh. In addition, a thinning of the subcutaneous tissue thickness in the vascular alteration topography was also noticed, but without intramuscular or bone extension.

Case Information: A one-year-old girl was brought to our center due to delays in neurodevelopment, bilateral hearing loss, and visual issues. Her parents are first cousins. The perinatal history was without complications. Physical examination showed normal growth parameters. She had bilateral hearing loss and was using hearing aids. The liver was palpable 6 cm below the right costal margin. Notable facial features included arched eyebrows, a broad nasal root, low set ears, downward slanting eyes, epicanthal folds, strabismus, and a myopathic face. Laboratory tests showed ALT at 101 U/L (normal range: 0–37) and AST at 53 U/L (normal range: 0–41). An ophthalmologic examination indicated septooptic dysplasia, with a pale optic disc and irregular optic disc margins. Visual evoked potentials demonstrated bilateral elongated P100 latency. Cranial MRI revealed nonspecific gliosis in the subcortical and periventricular deep white matter, and the superior margin of the sella had a mildly upward convexity. Analysis of very long chain fatty acids showed elevated C26:0, low C24:0, low C22:0, an elevated C26:0/C22:0 ratio, and highly elevated levels of phytanic acid and pristanic acid.
Diagnostic Tests: Molecular genetic analysis for PEX genes indicated homozygous novel IVS1-2A>G mutation in the PEX1 gene.

Case Information: A 51-year-old male presented with several months of progressively worsening headaches, visual disturbances, and gait imbalance. Physical examination revealed papilledema and poor tandem gait. A CT scan showed obstructive hydrocephalus, and an MRI scan revealed a large right cerebellopontine angle (CPA) mass with significant compression of the adjacent medulla and pons and obstructive hydrocephalus with a patent aqueduct. A right retrosigmoid approach was performed with intraoperative monitoring, including cranial nerve (CN) V, VII, X, and XII EMG monitoring, CN VII and X motor evoked potentials, bilateral brainstem auditory evoked responses, four-limb somatosensory evoked potentials, and motor evoked potentials. Intraoperatively, some tumor tissue was sent for frozen section pathology, which suggested some ependymal-type cells. As the tumor was found to encase multiple nerves, including CN VII, X, and XII, a decision was made to only attempt subtotal resection. The intraoperative monitoring did not suggest any significant changes, and the patient was intact.
Diagnostic Tests: The sections show a paucicellular tumor composed of small clusters of glial cells embedded in a dense fibrillar network. The tumor nuclei are uniformly small and round with fine dispersed chromatin and no discernable mitotic activity. Necrosis and microvascular proliferation are absent. Immunohistochemistry reveals strong cytoplasmic GFAP immunoreactivity and a Ki67 proliferation index of less than 1%.

Case Information: A 49-year-old female patient presented with numbness in her fingers that gradually extended to her entire body above the bellybutton over a period of six months. Her medical history included rapidly growing cutaneous neurofibromas on her back and left thigh over five years, which were surgically removed at a local hospital. Histological analysis confirmed these were neurofibromas with malignant characteristics. Physical examination revealed widespread café-au-lait spots, axillary and groin freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, and surgical scars on her back and left thigh. A sensory deficit was noted between the C4 level and the bellybutton. No iris hamartomas were detected, and the mammary glands were normal. Her mother and maternal grandmother exhibited similar features, but her daughter and sons showed no clinical signs of NF1.
Diagnostic Tests: Magnetic resonance imaging showed a relative-demarcated, heterogeneously enhanced mass lesion accompanied by perifocal edema in C5-7 level, a left-sided T11 spinous process heterogeneously enhanced mass in soft tissue, intervertebral disk hernia in L2-5 level and widespread punctum enhancing lesion in her scalp and in T11-L5 level. No evidences of optic pathway glioma and neurofibromatosis 2 (NF2) had been found in head MRI.

Case Information: A 42-year-old Caucasian male presented with a history of progressive fatigue, chills, night sweats, and unintended weight loss. Physical examination revealed left cervical lymphadenopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed widespread adenopathy, numerous small sclerotic lesions throughout the bones, and one small lucent lesion on the right side of the pelvis. An excisional biopsy of the cervical lymph node was performed. Histologic evaluation of the excised lymph node revealed effaced architecture with many atypical cells, including those with 'horseshoe/kidney'-shaped nuclei. The neoplastic cells were immuno-reactive for CD30, ALK (diffuse, cytoplasmic), CD2, CD4, granzyme B, and TIA-1. Many background CD68+ histiocytes were observed.
Diagnostic Tests: A bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed extensive disease.

Case Information: A 63-year-old Caucasian female with a history of diabetes mellitus reported a progressively enlarging cutaneous nodule in the lower mid-back region. She did not experience trauma, skin discharge, weight loss, fever, or night chills but did report mild fatigue. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed a diffuse abnormal signal over an area measuring approximately 11 cm × 8 cm. Ultrasound examination of the region demonstrated asymmetric abnormal echogenicity to the right of the midline.
Diagnostic Tests: Computed tomography–guided skin biopsy demonstrated a diffuse infiltration of malignant cells of moderate size with ovoid to irregular nuclear contours and many nucleoli with significant mitotic activity. Flow cytometric analysis identified an abnormal population of cells accounting for the majority of events analyzed, showing surface lambda light chain restriction; coexpression of CD19, CD20, FMC-7, and HLA-DR; and aberrant coexpression of both CD10 and CD5. Immunohistochemical stains for CD20, CD10, BCL2, MUM1, and c-MYC were strongly positive, BCL6 was moderately positive, and the malignant cells had a proliferation index (Ki-67) of greater than 90%. CD3 and Cyclin D1 were negative. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis was performed using DNA probes for aggressive B-cell lymphoma. Two hundred interphase nuclei were examined for each probe and revealed a rearrangement of the MYC gene in 93.5%, a rearrangement of the BCL6 gene in 97.5%, and a gain of BCL2/18q21 in 69.5% of nuclei. There was no evidence of a BCL2 gene rearrangement.
